title: Dan Ives Announces Boosting AI Stocks: Key Insight That Investors Can’t Miss】
body:
The technology sector’s most vocal skeptics were taken aback on Monday when Dan Ives, the veteran analyst at Wedbush Securities, highlighted a surge of underlying demand for artificial‑intelligence hardware and services that runs counter to the recent market tumble. While AI‑related equities have been battered by a wave of profit‑taking and macro‑headwinds, Ives pointed to fresh order books from Nvidia, a record‑setting partnership pipeline at Google Cloud, and a surprisingly robust pre‑IPO interest in Anthropic as evidence that the AI boom is far from over.

Ives’ commentary came as the Nasdaq’s AI‑heavy index slipped more than 8 % over the past two weeks, dragging down marquee names such as Nvidia (NVDA), Microsoft (MSFT) and Alphabet’s (GOOGL) cloud division. The sell‑off, he explained, is largely a reaction to elevated valuation multiples and heightened expectations rather than a fundamental shift in demand. “What we’re seeing is a classic over‑reaction to short‑term earnings noise,” Ives said, “while the long‑term growth trajectory remains intact.” He cited three data points that, in his view, underscore the resilience of the AI ecosystem.

First, Nvidia’s latest earnings release revealed that its “foundry‑in‑a‑box” platform, which bundles custom GPUs with software stacks for generative AI, has already secured orders worth more than $12 billion for the upcoming fiscal year. The company’s “DGX Cloud” service, now available through major hyperscalers, is projected to generate $3 billion in recurring revenue by 2028. Even after accounting for a modest 5 % year‑over‑year decline in the quarter’s gross margin, the sheer volume of committed spend suggests that enterprises are still racing to embed AI into core operations.

Second, Google Cloud disclosed that its AI‑accelerated infrastructure, built around the company’s custom Tensor Processing Units (TPUs), attracted a record $9 billion in new contracts during the quarter. The cloud provider’s “AI Studio” platform, which offers pre‑trained models and fine‑tuning tools, is now the preferred choice for more than 30 % of Fortune 500 firms seeking to deploy large‑language models at scale. Ives noted that the breadth of these engagements—spanning finance, healthcare, and manufacturing—demonstrates that AI adoption is moving beyond experimental pilots to production‑grade workloads.

Third, the filing for Anthropic’s initial public offering revealed that the startup has already secured $1.2 billion in committed capital from a consortium of institutional investors, including a $500 million anchor from a sovereign wealth fund. The company’s “Claude” model, positioned as a safer alternative to OpenAI’s flagship, has attracted interest from regulated sectors that require tighter control over hallucination and bias. Ives argued that Anthropic’s ability to raise such capital amid a market downturn signals confidence that the next wave of generative AI applications will be monetized more effectively than earlier iterations.

Analysts across the board are now recalibrating their forecasts. Wedbush has lifted its 12‑month price target for Nvidia to $1,200, up from $950, reflecting an anticipated 25 % increase in AI‑related hardware spend. Meanwhile, Morgan Stanley’s tech team upgraded Google Cloud’s revenue outlook, citing a 20 % acceleration in AI‑driven consumption. Even more cautiously optimistic, Credit Suisse’s research note highlighted that the “AI‑centric capital allocation” trend could sustain a 7‑10 % annual growth rate for the broader semiconductor and cloud services markets through 2030.

Nevertheless, investors are warned to remain vigilant. Supply‑chain constraints, especially the global shortage of advanced silicon wafers, could throttle the ability of manufacturers to meet the burgeoning order flow. Additionally, regulatory scrutiny over data privacy and model transparency is intensifying, with the European Union poised to enact stricter AI governance rules later this year. Ives cautioned that “while the top‑line demand is solid, execution risk remains, and companies that can navigate both operational and compliance challenges will emerge as the true winners.”

Looking ahead, the convergence of high‑performance hardware, scalable cloud platforms, and increasingly sophisticated AI models appears set to drive a new era of digital transformation. If the current wave of commitments translates into sustained revenue, the sector could rebound sharply from its recent dip, offering investors a compelling entry point. As the market digests these signals, the focus will shift from short‑term price volatility to the longer‑term narrative of AI becoming an indispensable utility across every industry.
